clinicalPearls: WHO grade 1 tumour that is the characteristic CNS neoplasm of tuberous sclerosis complex, arising near the foramen of Monro at the caudothalamic groove.

Typically presents in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood with signs of obstructive hydrocephalus: worsening headache, morning vomiting, papilloedema, decline in behaviour or cognition, or an increase in seizures.
Growth of a subependymal lesion on serial imaging, or a lesion of sufficient size near the foramen of Monro, distinguishes a SEGA from a static subependymal nodule.
Driven by biallelic loss of TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) with constitutive activation of the mTOR complex 1 pathway.
mTOR inhibitors (for example everolimus) can reduce tumour volume and are an option for lesions not requiring emergency surgery.
Surgical resection is definitive and is indicated for acute or symptomatic hydrocephalus.
Regular surveillance MRI is recommended in tuberous sclerosis complex to detect enlarging lesions before they cause hydrocephalus.
Discovery of a SEGA should prompt evaluation for the wider features of tuberous sclerosis complex.
reference.pathophysiology: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is a benign glioneuronal-astrocytic tumour that arises in tuberous sclerosis complex from the subependyma of the lateral ventricle adjacent to the foramen of Monro, characteristically at the caudothalamic groove. It results from biallelic inactivation of TSC1 (encoding hamartin, on chromosome 9q34) or TSC2 (encoding tuberin, on chromosome 16p13.3); loss of the hamartin-tuberin complex removes inhibition of Rheb and leads to constitutive activation of mTOR complex 1, driving cell growth and proliferation. The tumour is composed of large ganglion-like and plump gemistocyte-like astrocytic cells with variable calcification, and its periventricular location predisposes to obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid outflow and hydrocephalus.
additionalDifferentials: Subependymal nodule (non-growing) of tuberous sclerosis complex
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showing an enhancing, often calcified mass at the foramen of Monro, compared with prior imaging to assess for growth
CT to demonstrate calcification and ventricular size
Surveillance neuroimaging as part of tuberous sclerosis complex follow-up
Genetic testing for TSC1 and TSC2 mutations

Assessment for other tuberous sclerosis complex features (skin, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, retinal hamartoma) with echocardiography, renal imaging and dermatological/ophthalmological review
Histopathology with immunohistochemistry where the lesion is resected
redFlags: New or worsening headache, vomiting or papilloedema indicating obstructive hydrocephalus
Documented interval growth of a subependymal lesion near the foramen of Monro
Acute deterioration in conscious level from acute hydrocephalus
New focal deficit or a marked change in seizure pattern or behaviour
reference.prognosis: As a WHO grade 1 tumour the prognosis is good, with the main morbidity arising from obstructive hydrocephalus. Outcomes are favourable with timely surgery or mTOR-inhibitor therapy, though lesions may regrow and warrant ongoing surveillance.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a growing SEGA as a stable subependymal nodule and missing impending hydrocephalus.
Assuming that absence of an obvious tuberous sclerosis complex phenotype excludes the diagnosis; rare cases occur without full clinical features.
Delaying surveillance imaging in tuberous sclerosis complex until symptoms develop.
Attributing new headaches or behavioural change solely to epilepsy rather than raised intracranial pressure.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Central Nervous System Tumours
International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex consensus and surveillance guidelines
